assets.title: Sensor Placement, Dew Point & Canopy Microclimates
assets.altText: Educational canopy diagram comparing representative crop-plane sensors with biased room locations and explaining dew-point condensation risk and transition logging.
assets.teachingPurpose: Teach that environmental readings are spatial and time-dependent; explain placement bias, canopy microclimates, dew point, transition logging and sensor verification.
expandedScience: A sensor can be accurate at its own location while failing to represent the canopy because walls, HVAC outlets, humidifiers, lights, doors and foliage create gradients.
Dense foliage can create leaf-zone temperature, humidity and air-movement conditions that differ materially from room-average measurements.
Condensation risk rises as a plant surface approaches the air dew-point temperature; dew point reflects atmospheric water-vapor content and temperature rather than a universal crop target.
Transition periods such as lights-off, irrigation and humidification can create short-lived conditions hidden by daily averages.
Sensor location, crop-plane height, instrument identity, timestamp and verification state should remain attached to the reading.

assets.title: Container Water Distribution & Sensor Placement
assets.altText: Container cross-section showing emitter wetting pattern, roots, local moisture gradients, representative and biased sensor positions, drainage and post-irrigation water-status change.
assets.teachingPurpose: Explain spatial water distribution, local sensor bias, water-content versus water-availability concepts and why dryback needs a defined metric and method.
expandedScience: Container water status is spatial because irrigation pattern, substrate structure, geometry, root occupancy and drainage create horizontal and vertical gradients.
A probe reports its local environment and may systematically misrepresent the crop when it sits beside an emitter, wall, container bottom, saturated pocket or unrooted area.
Volumetric water content describes amount of water present, while matric forces and salinity influence how difficult that water is for roots to acquire.
The post-irrigation curve contains drainage, redistribution, evaporation and plant water use; the entire decline should not automatically be attributed to plant uptake.
Dryback comparisons require the measurement metric, units, start and end points, sensor position, substrate and timing.

assets.title: IPM Scouting & Differential Diagnosis
assets.altText: Educational IPM diagram showing a repeatable scouting route, spatial symptom patterns, differential evidence board and evidence-based decision workflow.
assets.teachingPurpose: Make scouting repeatable and teach learners to use pattern, supporting and conflicting evidence, confirmation steps and trend data before assigning a diagnosis.
expandedScience: Repeatable scouting should inspect new growth, leaf undersides, stems, media surfaces and monitoring cards using the same route and sampling unit through time.
Spatial patterns can help distinguish localized biological spread from irrigation-zone, edge, light-footprint or room-wide abiotic patterns.
A useful differential separates observation, supporting evidence, conflicting evidence and the next confirmation step rather than jumping directly from symptom to cause.
Detection does not automatically equal treatment; crop stage, population or disease trend, risk and legally available controls influence the action threshold.
Plant or zone identity, date, counts including zero counts, images, context, intervention and follow-up should remain in the record.
